prompt: What distinguishes an API gateway from a plain reverse proxy?

options.text: It caches every response body so services rarely see repeat traffic
It understands APIs: routes, keys, users, quotas and versions
It spreads traffic evenly across identical copies of one service
It resolves service names to IPs, replacing DNS inside the cluster

explanation: A gateway is an API-aware reverse proxy: it routes by API path and knows about keys, users, quotas and versions. (a) Caching is something many proxies do; it isn't what makes a gateway. (c) describes a load balancer, which the lesson warns is a different thing. (d) Service discovery and DNS are separate infrastructure; a gateway doesn't replace them.

prompt: Why route at the gateway instead of letting clients call services directly?

options.text: Services can be split, moved or versioned without changing clients
Each extra hop through the gateway lowers backend response times
Services no longer need their own authorisation or ownership checks
Clients get one connection per service, which spreads load evenly

explanation: Routing hides the internal layout, so you can split, move or version services without shipping new clients. (b) An extra hop adds latency; it doesn't speed services up. (c) is the lesson's top misconception: the gateway proves identity but services still authorise. (d) is backwards: the client talks to one gateway endpoint, not one connection per service.

scenario: A gateway verifies JWTs and forwards `X-User-Id`. The orders service trusts the header and cancels any order ID it receives. User 42 cancels user 77's order by changing the ID in the URL.

options.text: JWTs can't be trusted once verified at the gateway; each service must re-verify the signature itself
The orders service must still check that the user owns the order; the gateway only proves identity
The gateway should switch to API keys, which are tied to an account and so stop cross-user access
Nothing is wrong; once the gateway has authenticated the caller, every request it forwards is allowed

explanation: Authentication at the edge, authorisation in the service: only orders knows who owns order 991, so it must check ownership. (a) Verifying at the gateway is fine; re-verifying the token still wouldn't tell you who owns the order. (c) API keys also only identify the caller, so the same hole remains. (d) is exactly the misconception that caused the bug.

prompt: What must the gateway do with an `X-User-Id` header sent by the client?

options.text: Forward it unchanged so services can see who the client says it is
Strip it and set its own value from the verified credential
Keep it if it matches a real user ID, otherwise reject the call
Append the verified ID next to it and let services pick one

explanation: The gateway must strip any client-supplied identity header and set its own from the verified credential. (a) lets any client impersonate anyone. (c) A real user ID is still someone else's ID; existence isn't ownership. (d) leaves the forged value in the request, and services may read the wrong one.

prompt: Which concerns usually belong in the gateway? Select all that apply.

options.text: TLS termination for all public traffic
Per-API-key rate limiting and quotas
Calculating an order's discount total
Attaching a trace ID to each request

explanation: Shared, business-free concerns go in the gateway: TLS (a), per-key rate limits (b) and trace IDs (d). Discounts (c) need business data and rules, so they belong in a service.

prompt: Roughly how long does the gateway-aggregated call take?
scenario: A phone has a 100 ms round trip to your data centre. The home screen needs 4 services taking 30, 50, 120 and 20 ms. The gateway calls all four in parallel.

options.text: About 640 ms
About 230 ms
About 100 ms
About 50 ms

explanation: One phone round trip (100 ms) plus the slowest parallel call (120 ms) plus small internal hops ≈ 230 ms. (a) adds every call as if they ran sequentially, plus extra round trips. (c) counts only the round trip and ignores the service work. (d) ignores the round trip, and parallel calls finish when the slowest one does, not the fastest.

prompt: How do you stop one slow dependency from slowing an aggregated response?

options.text: Call services one after another so a slow one is easier to spot
Set a per-dependency timeout and return a partial response
Wait for every dependency, then retry the slowest one at once
Raise the gateway's overall timeout so all calls can finish

explanation: A per-dependency timeout bounds the wait, and the screen renders without the slow part. (a) Sequential calls make total latency the sum, which is worse. (c) Waiting then retrying adds even more delay. (d) A longer timeout just lets the slow dependency hold the whole response longer.

scenario: Your shared gateway has grown hundreds of rules like 'if TV app, add 4K artwork; if iOS v3, drop field X'. Every client team waits on the gateway team to ship.

options.text: Keep one shared gateway but add more per-client if-statements
A backend for frontend per client type, owned by each client team
Let each client call the services directly and shape data itself
Move the per-client rules into every backend service instead

explanation: BFFs let each client team shape its own data without coordinating every change through one team. (a) is the problem being described. (c) loses the gateway's shared concerns and forces many round trips over slow networks. (d) spreads client-specific logic into every service, so every client change now touches many teams.

prompt: What most helps a gateway avoid being a single point of failure?

options.text: One large instance with lots of headroom so it never runs out of capacity
Several stateless instances across zones, with shared state in Redis
Several instances, each keeping its own rate-limit counters in memory
Pushing every config change to all instances at once to keep them in sync

explanation: Redundancy plus statelessness: several instances across zones, with shared state such as rate-limit counters in a store like Redis. (a) One instance is a single point of failure no matter how big. (c) Per-instance counters make limits inconsistent and lose state when an instance dies. (d) A bad config rolled everywhere at once takes every instance down; rollouts should be gradual.

prompt: Two independent gateway instances each have 99.9% availability. What is the best-case availability of the pair?
explanation: The pair is down only when both are down: 0.001 × 0.001 = 0.000001, so 99.9999%. (a) ignores the redundancy. (b) adds two nines instead of the three that multiplying the failure probabilities gives. (d) overshoots by a nine; two instances can't do better than the product of their failure rates. Correlated failures make the real number lower.
